issues.legal_issue: A plaint may be amended before trial to add particulars supporting an existing claim, including by adding persons connected with the alleged payments, when the amendment does not change the cause of action or unfairly prejudice the opposing party.
material_facts: The suit sought specific performance of an agreement concerning a share in property and alleged that consideration had been paid.
The original plaint asserted that the full consideration under the agreement had been paid but did not set out the details of how the money was paid.
The amendment sought to explain the mode of payment and to add proposed plaintiffs and defendants associated with the payments.
The amendment application was filed before trial commenced.

The courts below allowed only part of the requested amendment, and the Supreme Court found that the permitted changes supplied details supporting the existing payment contention without changing the cause of action or prejudicing the defendants.
issues.conclusion: The amendment was properly allowed to the extent permitted by the courts below; it supplied supporting details rather than changing the cause of action, and the objection that the proposed plaintiffs were not parties to the agreement did not warrant setting aside that order.
issues.legal_principle: Order VI Rules 2 and 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 require pleadings to state material facts and authorize just amendments necessary to determine the real questions in controversy. Amendment is not a matter of right, but courts should generally adopt a liberal rather than hyper-technical approach to bona fide, legitimate and necessary amendments, particularly where prejudice can be compensated by costs. The court should consider whether the amendment changes the nature of the case, introduces a new cause of action, causes irremediable prejudice, or defeats limitation. These principles are drawn from Rajkumar Gurawara (Dead) Through L.Rs. v. S.K. Sarwagi & Company Private Limited and Revajeetu Builders & Developers v. Narayanaswamy & Sons. Order I Rule 1 concerns who may be joined as plaintiffs.

rule.if: civil_suit_amendment_application and filed_before_trial and original_pleading_laid_foundation and amendment_adds_supporting_payment_details and does_not_change_cause_of_action and does_not_cause_irremediable_prejudice

predicates.civil_suit_amendment_application: A party applied to amend pleadings in a civil suit.
predicates.filed_before_trial: The amendment application was filed before the trial commenced.
predicates.original_pleading_laid_foundation: The original pleading already stated the essential basis of the claim that the proposed amendment supported.
predicates.amendment_adds_supporting_payment_detail: The proposed amendment adds particulars about how payments relating to the existing claim were made.
predicates.does_not_change_cause_of_action: The proposed amendment does not introduce a different cause of action.
predicates.does_not_cause_irremediable_prejudice: Allowing the amendment does not cause the opposing party prejudice that cannot be adequately remedied.

issues.definition: When an amendment application in a civil suit is made before trial to add supporting payment details to a claim already founded in the pleading, without changing the cause of action or causing irremediable prejudice, the amendment is permissible.

issues.legal_issue: An amendment that only supplies further particulars supporting an existing claim is not barred by limitation merely because those particulars are added after the original pleading.
material_facts: The original plaint alleged that the full consideration under the agreement had been paid but did not explain the mode of payment.
The proposed amendment supplied details of payments made before the agreement and alleged that the payments were made through nominees and treated as payments to the contracting defendant.
The Supreme Court concluded that the amendment explained the existing payment contention and did not alter the cause of action.
issues.conclusion: The amendment was not barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, limitation is a relevant consideration in deciding an amendment application; as stated in Revajeetu Builders & Developers v. Narayanaswamy & Sons, courts should generally decline an amendment if a fresh suit on the amended claim would be barred by limitation on the date of the application. Here, the amendment supplied particulars supporting the existing claim and did not introduce a new cause of action, so the limitation objection failed.
